# Xenon Choir

A Pen created on CodePen.

Original URL: [https://codepen.io/editor/Chirag-Ns/pen/01a17d81-ef6e-705a-b6e8-a2bec03a865e](https://codepen.io/editor/Chirag-Ns/pen/01a17d81-ef6e-705a-b6e8-a2bec03a865e).

Five spectrum tubes on a dark shelf: helium, neon, argon, krypton and xenon. Each tube glows in the color its own light makes on the eye. The emission lines of each gas, with wavelengths and strengths from the NIST line tables, are run through the CIE 1931 color matching functions, so helium comes out pink, neon orange red, argon violet, krypton lavender and xenon blue.

The lightning inside grows by the dielectric breakdown model. The discharge is a tree held at zero potential, the far electrode sits at one, Laplace's equation is solved on a lattice, and at every step one cell joins the tree with a probability set by the local field. When the tree reaches the other electrode the channel flashes and the tube lights up.

Every gas also sings. Each of its strongest emission lines is shifted down by exactly forty octaves (the frequency of the light divided by 2^40) and becomes one voice of a chord. Neon's chord is neon's light, forty octaves lower. The five tubes make a choir: they come in one by one, sing together at the thirty second mark, then go quiet.

Move the pointer over a tube, or touch it, and the lightning comes to your finger. Press M or use the button in the corner for sound. All the audio is made live in the browser, no samples.
